steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on FM-MCVRP, a foundation model for the Montreal Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem. Cover the state of CVRP research in OR, the rise of ML and deep learning for routing, then a "Contributions of This Work" subsection and the outline of the paper.

steps.text:

2. OR solution methods: exact, heuristic, metaheuristic
3. ML successes and ML/DL for routing problems
## 1.1 Contributions of This Work
4. Four contributions: LLM framework, unified model, outperforming training solutions, generalization
5. Paper structure

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. CVRP research
- one of most well-researched CO problems in OR, transportation, logistics; many commercial / non-commercial applications
- two directions: (a) new methods, more efficient, larger instances, new best known solutions to benchmarks; (b) new, more advanced variants from industry challenges, extra constraints

2. OR methods
- (i) exact incl. MP, (ii) heuristics, (iii) metaheuristics
- MP dominant exact method; NP-hard -> intractable for realistic sizes
- large-scale industrial instances: heuristics / metaheuristics
- LKH-3 heuristic and HGS among best performing for CVRP

3. ML
- ML dominated CV and NLP; applications from strategic game playing to molecular biology
- generative AI like ChatGPT: human-like conversations
- extremely large state space -> can ML complement or replace OR methods for CO?
- PN: NN approximates TSP solutions; inspired many DL routing approaches
- not new: Hopfield network solved small TSP instances

## 1.1 Contributions of This Work
4a. LLM advances -> CO in transportation/logistics
- FM-MCVRP: supervised DL model, near-optimal solutions to MCVRP (CVRP variant mimicking real-world delivery problems)
- prior work: Transformer in PN framework; ours first DL model using Transformer in LLM framework for routing
- built on T5 (mostly NLP); routing as analogous NLP task, predict nodes on fixed graph, no PN

4b. Unified model
- range of problem sizes and vehicle capacities -> real-world applicability
- previous works: one model per size/capacity combination; impractical for companies
- ours up to 800-node instances vs up to 100-node (training divergence, Appendix C); real last-mile problems > 100 customers

4c. Outperforms training solutions
- strong managerial implications; companies lack expertise to invest in tailored algorithms; rely on simple algorithms, decision rules, human experience
- amass potentially sub-optimal route sequences (algorithmic or observed from drivers)
- FM-MCVRP agnostic to how training solutions obtained -> improve routes from existing data, no explicit algorithm
- competitive with / may beat state-of-the-art benchmarks on some instances despite inferior, inexpensive training solutions

4d. Generalization
- train on 20 to 400-node, test on 600 and 800-node; keeps favorable performance
- stops per route vary with commercial, geographical, operational context (product/customer characteristics, stop density, vehicle technology)
- skewed training data still fine; plan routes as demand profile / operational context changes

5. Structure
- Sec 2 literature (exact, heuristics/metaheuristics, DL, decoding strategies); Sec 3 CVRP + MCVRP definitions; Sec 4 methodology + model; Sec 5 setup; Sec 6 results; Sec 7 managerial insights; Sec 8 summary + future research

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The CVRP is one of the most well-researched CO problems in the OR, transportation, and logistics literature, because it has many commercial and non-commercial applications. Even today it is still an active area of academic research, and advances are being made in two main directions. First, researchers try to develop new methods, either to solve existing variants of the problem more efficiently and for larger problem instances, or to find new best known solutions to benchmark problem instances from the literature. Second, motivated by the more and more sophisticated routing challenges in the transportation and logistics industry, authors define and study new and more advanced variants of the problem that capture additional constraints and nuanced problem characteristics.

In terms of methods, the OR literature on the CVRP and its many variants can be grouped into (i) exact methods, including MP, (ii) heuristic approaches, and (iii) metaheuristic approaches. MP is the dominant exact method for solving CO problems like the CVRP. But because these problems are NP-hard, such models quickly become intractable for problem instances of realistic size. So for the large-scale problem instances that often come up in real industrial applications, most state-of-the-art solution methods use heuristic and metaheuristic approaches. In particular, the LKH-3 heuristic from prior work and HGS are currently among the best performing solution approaches to the CVRP.

ML methods, on the other hand, have dominated the fields of CV and NLP in recent years. ML has also found many highly visible applications, from strategic game playing to molecular biology. More recently, generative AI models that are publicly discussed, such as ChatGPT, have made human-like conversations with a machine possible. The algorithmic performance is advancing quickly and keeps pushing the boundaries of the state-of-the-art results that can be achieved. Since these problems generally have an extremely large state space, a natural next question is how far ML can be applied to CO problems and complement or even replace existing OR methods. In particular, PN, which were first proposed in, show how a NN can approximate solutions to the TSP. This work has since inspired many approaches to solving routing problems with DL. The idea of using NN to solve CO problems like the TSP is not entirely new though. For example, one earlier work was the first to solve small TSP instances with a so-called Hopfield network.

## 1.1 Contributions of This Work

- First: LLM advances applied to routing; FM-MCVRP, supervised DL model for the MCVRP (mimics real-world delivery problems)
  - prior Transformer + PN work vs ours: first Transformer in LLM framework for routing; built on T5, routing as analogous NLP task on fixed graph, no PN
- Second: unified model for range of sizes and capacities
  - previous works: one model per size/capacity combination, impractical for companies
  - up to 800-node vs up to 100-node (training divergence, Appendix C); last-mile problems > 100 customers
- Third: outperforms the solutions it was trained on
  - companies rely on simple algorithms, rules, experience; collect potentially sub-optimal routes
  - agnostic to how training solutions are obtained; improve routes from existing data
  - competitive with / may beat state-of-the-art benchmarks despite inferior training solutions
- Fourth: generalization; train 20 to 400-node, test 600 and 800-node
  - stops per route vary by context; skewed training data; changing demand profile
- Structure: Sections 2-8

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The CVRP is one of the most well-researched CO problems in the OR, transportation, and logistics literature, because it has many commercial and non-commercial applications. Even today it is still an active area of academic research, and advances are being made in two main directions. First, researchers try to develop new methods, either to solve existing variants of the problem more efficiently and for larger problem instances, or to find new best known solutions to benchmark problem instances from the literature. Second, motivated by the more and more sophisticated routing challenges in the transportation and logistics industry, authors define and study new and more advanced variants of the problem that capture additional constraints and nuanced problem characteristics.

In terms of methods, the OR literature on the CVRP and its many variants can be grouped into (i) exact methods, including MP, (ii) heuristic approaches, and (iii) metaheuristic approaches. MP is the dominant exact method for solving CO problems like the CVRP. But because these problems are NP-hard, such models quickly become intractable for problem instances of realistic size. So for the large-scale problem instances that often come up in real industrial applications, most state-of-the-art solution methods use heuristic and metaheuristic approaches. In particular, the LKH-3 heuristic from prior work and HGS are currently among the best performing solution approaches to the CVRP.

ML methods, on the other hand, have dominated the fields of CV and NLP in recent years. ML has also found many highly visible applications, from strategic game playing to molecular biology. More recently, generative AI models that are publicly discussed, such as ChatGPT, have made human-like conversations with a machine possible. The algorithmic performance is advancing quickly and keeps pushing the boundaries of the state-of-the-art results that can be achieved. Since these problems generally have an extremely large state space, a natural next question is how far ML can be applied to CO problems and complement or even replace existing OR methods. In particular, PN, which were first proposed in, show how a NN can approximate solutions to the TSP. This work has since inspired many approaches to solving routing problems with DL. The idea of using NN to solve CO problems like the TSP is not entirely new though. For example, one earlier work was the first to solve small TSP instances with a so-called Hopfield network.

## 1.1 Contributions of This Work

This work has four main contributions. First, we show that recent methodological advances in the field of LLM can be applied successfully to solving combinatorial optimization problems in the transportation and logistics domain, such as vehicle routing. We propose the FM-MCVRP, a new supervised DL model that approximates near-optimal solutions to the MCVRP, which is a particularly relevant variant of the CVRP that mimics many real-world delivery problems. Recent work and builds on the Transformer architecture in a PN framework, but FM-MCVRP is, to the best of our knowledge, the first DL model that uses the Transformer architecture in an LLM framework for routing problems. We build on the T5 model, which has mostly been applied to NLP problems, and model the routing problem as an analogous NLP task that predicts the nodes to visit defined on a fixed graph, instead of using a PN.

Second, our model is a unified model that accepts a range of problem sizes and vehicle capacities. This makes it very applicable to real-world problems, instead of only doing well on stylized problem instances with tightly controlled parameters. Previous works, such as and, train a single model for each combination of problem size and vehicle capacity. This seems impractical for real-world operations, because companies cannot manage a large number of ML models trained for every possible combination of problem size and capacity they might see. Also, our model can solve problem instances with up to 800 nodes, while and solve only up to 100-node problem instances, because larger instances make the training process diverge (see Appendix C). But many real-world delivery problems, especially in last-mile logistics, have more than 100 customers.

Third, we show that our model can outperform the algorithmically obtained solutions it was trained on. This has strong managerial implications. Many real-world routing problems are large and complex, and many companies lack the expertise and ability to invest in high-performing algorithms tailored to their specific problem, so they rely on route planning tools based on fairly simple algorithms, decision rules, and human experience. So many companies keep collecting large amounts of route sequences that are possibly sub-optimal, obtained either algorithmically or by watching how drivers actually execute routes. The FM-MCVRP does not care which method was used to get the solutions it is trained on, so it lets companies improve route quality by using the routing data they already have. This means they can gradually improve their routes by learning from available data, without investing in designing and maintaining an explicit algorithm tailored to their business needs. Our model can find solutions that are competitive with, and on certain problem instances may even outperform, state-of-the-art benchmark methods, even though it was trained on inferior but computationally inexpensive solutions.

Fourth, we show that FM-MCVRP generalizes well to larger problem instances. We train the model on problem instances with 20 to 400 nodes and then test it on 600 and 800-node problem instances. FM-MCVRP consistently keeps its favorable performance on these larger instances. Being able to generalize to larger instance sizes not seen before while keeping a high solution quality matters a lot for many real-world routing problems. The number of stops on a route can vary a lot depending on the commercial, geographical, and operational context (e.g., product and customer characteristics, stop density, vehicle technology, etc.). A company's training data may be skewed towards some instance sizes, but the trained FM-MCVRP can still give good results for instance sizes that are unseen or less common. In the same way, a company could train FM-MCVRP on historical data from routes it runs now and use the trained model to plan routes even when the demand profile of its clients or the operational and technological context of its routes changes over time.

The rest of the paper is structured like this. Section 2 reviews the literature on solving or approximating solutions to the CVRP, covering exact methods, heuristics and metaheuristics, DL approaches, and decoding strategies for DL approaches. Section 3 formally defines the CVRP and revisits the formal definition of the MCVRP presented in. Section 4 explains our methodology and presents the FM-MCVRP model. Section 5 describes the setup of the computational experiments, and Section 6 presents the results and insights from them. Section 7 gives the managerial insights. Section 8 concludes with a summary of the work and what we see as fruitful directions for future research.

However, the NP-hard nature of these problems [4] quickly renders such models intractable for realistically sized problem instances. Therefore, for solving the large-scale problem instances often faced in real industrial applications, most state-of-the-art solution methods rely on heuristic and metaheuristic approaches [5,6]. Most notably, the LKH-3 heuristic by [7] and HGS [6] are currently among the best performing solution approaches to the CVRP [6].

ML methods, on the other hand, have dominated the fields of CV and NLP in recent years. ML has also found numerous highly visible applications, from strategic game playing [8] to molecular biology [9]. More recently, publicly discussed generative AI models such as ChatGPT have enabled human-like conversations with a machine. Rapidly advancing algorithmic performance is constantly pushing the boundaries of achievable state-of-the-art results. As these problems generally have an extremely large state space, a natural next question in research is to what extent ML can be applied to CO problems to complement or even replace existing OR methods [10]. Specifically, PN, first proposed by [11], demonstrate how a NN can approximate solutions to the TSP. This work has since inspired numerous approaches to solving routing problems with DL [12,13,14,15]. The idea of leveraging NN to solve CO problems such as the TSP is not entirely new, though. For instance, [16] were the first to solve small TSP instances with a so-called Hopfield network.

## 1.1 Contributions of This Work

There are four main contributions of this work. First, we show that recent methodological advances in the field of LLM can be successfully applied to solving combinatorial optimization problems in the transportation and logistics domain, such as vehicle routing. Specifically, we propose the FM-MCVRP, a novel supervised DL model that approximates near-optimal solutions to the MCVRP, a particularly relevant variant of the CVRP that mimics many real-world delivery problems [10]. Unlike recent work from [14] and [15], who build on the Transformer architecture [17] in a PN framework, FM-MCVRP is to the best of our knowledge the first DL model leveraging the Transformer architecture in an LLM framework for routing problems. Building on the T5 model by [18], which has largely been applied to NLP problems, we model the underlying routing problem as an analogous NLP task that predicts the nodes to visit defined on a fixed graph, instead of using a PN.

Second, our proposed model is a unified model that accepts a range of problem sizes and vehicle capacities. This makes it highly applicable to real-world problems, rather than only performing well on stylized problem instances with tightly controlled parameters. Previous works, such as [14] and [15], train a single model for each combination of problem size and vehicle capacity, which seems impractical for real-world operations, as companies do not have the capability to manage a large number of ML models trained for each possible combination of problem size and capacity they might encounter. Moreover, our proposed model can solve problem instances of up to 800 nodes, compared to [14] and [15], who solve up to 100-node problem instances since larger instances result in divergence in the training process (see Appendix C). However, many real-world delivery problems, especially in last-mile logistics, contain more than 100 customers.

Third, we show that our proposed model is able to outperform the algorithmically obtained solutions it was trained on. This finding has strong managerial implications. Given the size and complexity of many real-world routing problems, and lacking the expertise and ability to invest in high-performing algorithms explicitly tailored to their specific problem, many companies rely on route planning tools based on relatively simple algorithms, decision rules, and human experience. Hence, many companies continue to amass large quantities of potentially sub-optimal route sequences, obtained either algorithmically or by observing how routes are actually executed by drivers. Since the FM-MCVRP is agnostic to the method used to obtain the solutions on which it is trained, it allows companies to improve route quality by leveraging their existing routing data. They can thus gradually improve the quality of their routes by learning from readily available data, without having to invest in designing and maintaining an explicit algorithm tailored to their business needs. Notably, our model is able to find solutions that are competitive with, and on certain problem instances may even outperform, state-of-the-art benchmark methods, despite being trained on inferior yet computationally inexpensive solutions.

Fourth, we show that FM-MCVRP generalizes well to larger problem instances. Specifically, we train our model on 20 to 400-node problem instances and then test it on 600 and 800-node problem instances, and find that FM-MCVRP consistently maintains its favorable performance characteristics on these larger instances. The ability to generalize to larger, previously unseen instance sizes while maintaining high solution quality has important implications for many real-world routing problems. The number of stops on a route may vary widely depending on the commercial, geographical, and operational context (e.g., product and customer characteristics, stop density, vehicle technology, etc.). While a company’s training data may be skewed towards certain instance sizes, the trained FM-MCVRP can still yield good results for previously unseen or less prominent instance sizes. Similarly, a company may train FM-MCVRP on historical data from the routes it currently performs and leverage the trained model to plan routes even as the demand profile of its clients or the operational and technological context of its routes changes over time.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we review relevant literature for solving or approximating solutions to the CVRP, covering exact methods, heuristics and metaheuristics, DL approaches, and finally decoding strategies for DL approaches. In Section 3, we formally define the CVRP and revisit the formal definition of the MCVRP presented by [10]. In Section 4, we detail our methodology and present our FM-MCVRP model. In Section 5, we describe the setup of our computational experiments, and the results and insights from these experiments are presented in Section 6. In Section 7, we provide managerial insights. We conclude in Section 8 with a summary of our work and an overview of what we consider fruitful directions for future research.
